title: Effect of High Lithium Content on the Microstructure and Properties of Al-Mg-Si-Mn Casting Alloys
abstract: Abstract The widespread use of lithium-containing wrought aluminum alloys is attributed to their high mechanical strength combined with reduced density. Currently, Al-Cu-Li and Al-Mg-Li wrought alloys are regarded as promising materials for applications where low density is essential. Despite this, the development of lithium-containing casting aluminum alloys remains limited. In this study, the Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy was selected as the base material, with lithium additions ranging from 0.8 to 4.0 wt.%. The microstructure of the experimental alloys was characterized using macro- and microstructural analyses, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction, and mechanical testing to determine hardness and compressive yield strength. The addition of 2.1 wt.% lithium resulted in a complete change of the alloy structure from a fine-lamellar eutectic-type to coarser blocky intermetallics. This trend persisted in alloys with 2.5, 3.0, and 4.0 wt.% Li. The alloy with 4.0 wt.% lithium led to a significant increase in hardness, from 82 HV5 in the base alloy to 157 HV5. Compression tests demonstrated a similar improvement, with yield strength increasing from 135 MPa to 352 MPa in the as-cast condition. Tests conducted at 300 °C showed a gradual increase in yield strength from 124 MPa to 170 MPa at 4.0 wt.% lithium. These results demonstrate the strong potential of lithium-containing Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloys for foundry applications without the need for additional heat treatment.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Despite the various metallurgical challenges involved in producing Li-containing aluminum alloys, which arise from the high Li reactivity with aluminum melt and its strong tendency to oxidation, this innovative class of materials remains a focus of scientific and practical interest. The mainstream in this field is to develop alloys that not only exhibit high strength and stiffness, but also achieve a significant reduction in density, making them particularly suitable for a wide range of applications, especially in the aeronautical industry. 1 , 2  Numerous studies have focused on identifying suitable alloy compositions that utilize the strengthening effect of Li, as well as on examining the effects of production routes on the microstructure and, consequently, the mechanical properties of wrought Li-containing alloys. The successful applications of third-generation Al-Li alloys demonstrate improved thermal stability and toughness. In these alloys, the Li content decreased from 2.1 to 2.7 wt.% in the second generation to 1.0–1.8 wt.% in the third. 3  However, research on the design of Li-containing casting alloys is limited. Therefore, the ongoing search for alloy compositions that combine the benefits of Li addition with compatibility for shape casting remains an issue for both foundrymen and researchers.

A comprehensive review of the current state of research on Al-Li alloys is presented in the works of Rioja et al., 3  Hajjioui et al., 4  Prasad et al., 5 , 6  and Zou et al., 7  Numerous investigations dating back to the late 1980s 8 , 9  have enabled the design of Al alloys with Li. By using alloy 2219 (Al-Cu system, ~6.0 wt.% Cu) as the base material, Li addition was chosen to keep the composition within the field where the T1-Al 2 CuLi phase is more stable than δ′-Al 3 Li. Peak strength was achieved at 1.3 wt.% Li, where the level of ultimate tensile strength of 700 MPa was reached. Following the success of the Weldalite 049 alloy, designed by Gayle et al., 8  a large body of research has examined the structure and properties of wrought Li-containing alloys. Special attention has been paid to characterizing the precipitation process in these alloys. One of the most interesting features of T1 precipitates, which form in Al-Cu-based alloys via sequence SSSS⇒precursor phase⇒T1-Al 2 CuLi, is that they nucleate on dislocations. 10 , 11  Further addition of the alloying elements Mg, Ag, Mn, Sc, and Zr leads to the formation of several types of precipitates, namely Al 2 LiMg, Ω-Al 2 (Cu, Ag), or dispersoids β′-Al 3 Zr or Al 3 (Sc, Zr). When Cu is replaced by Mg, 12  the Al-2.5%Li-2%Mg-0.15%Zr-0.12%Ti alloy possessed an ultimate tensile strength of 417 MPa, which is slightly lower than that of the Al-Cu-Li system, but the alloy density reduced to − 2.52 g/cm 3 . Nevertheless, progress in developing Al-Li alloys suitable for shape casting remains very limited.

Although research on casting in the Al-Li system began in the 1920s, 4  it wasn’t until 1987 that one of the first papers addressing the interaction between Al-Li melts and mold materials was published. In the study conducted by Tong et al., 13  various Al-based alloys containing 2.5 wt.% Li, combined with Cu and Mg, were developed and analyzed to investigate its interaction with sand casting molds and used binders. The researchers examined factors such as alloy fluidity and the mechanical properties of the cast ingots. Their findings indicated that substituting the silicate binder with resin in the sand molds reduced interaction with the liquid alloy, achieving casting soundness comparable to that of iron permanent molds. Additionally, the fluidity of all Li-containing alloys, measured by the length of a spiral, was found to be lower than that of a commercial A356 alloy cast at the same overheating temperature. Notably, the Li-containing alloy containing Mg exhibited a greater spiral length in comparison with the alloy containing Cu, specifying the better fluidity of the Mg-containing alloy. When comparing the mechanical properties of Li-containing cast alloys to those of wrought materials, it was observed that the alloy cast in an iron mold and subjected to T6 heat treatment demonstrated a strength only 20 % lower than that of its wrought counterpart.

Following the development of the AlTiC grain refiner by A. Banerji and W. Reif in 1986, 14  Labarre et al., 15  and later Birch et al., 16  conducted a comparison of the grain refinement efficiency between AlTiB and AlTiC additions in Al-Li alloys. Their findings indicated that the AlTiC grain refiner reduces the grain size of the 8090 alloy (Al-Cu-Mg-Li system) more effectively than the AlTiB. Specifically, the addition of 0.4 wt.% of the AlTiC master alloy resulted in a significant reduction of the grain size to approximately 200 µm, with lower scattering in grain size compared to an equivalent addition of a Al3Ti1B master alloy. Recently, in the work of Boyko et al. 17  it was confirmed that the structure of the casting Al5Mg2SiMn-type casting alloy containing 1.2 wt.% Li can be refined with AlTi5B1 master alloy. The addition of 0.1 wt.% AlTi5B1 master alloy reduces the grain size from 260 µm to 150 µm, and the final structure of the cast specimens is fully equiaxed. In the early 1990 th , Chakravorty et al. 18  demonstrated that the addition of 0.8 wt.% of an Al3Ti1B grain refiner significantly reduces the grain size of the Al-2.7 wt.% Li alloy, transforming the as-cast structure from a columnar to a fine, equiaxed grain structure with an average size of 90 µm. Achieving a fine-grained structure in Li-containing alloys requires nearly four times as much grain refiner as for conventional alloys. A brief review of current techniques for controlling the structure formation of Li-containing aluminum casting alloys shows that identifying how to achieve a fine equiaxed grain structure conditions in castings remains underexplored and warrants further research.

In further research, it was found that during casting Al-2.7 wt.% Li in sand molds with a sodium-silicate binder, the liquid alloy reacts with the binder, forming a mineral phase, α-spodumene (LiAlSi 2 0 6 ), on the ingot’s surface. This reaction causes a loss of Li from the casting surface, reducing microhardness near the edges of the ingot. 19  Partridge reached a similar conclusion, 20  noting that during homogenization at a temperature of 543 °C in an open atmosphere, the depth of the Li-depleted zone on the surface of the alloy could extend up to 3 mm. Depletion of the surface of the cast part with Li makes heat treatment of Al-Li alloys somewhat challenging and requires an inert atmosphere. The authors also observed strong surface oxidation of Li-containing specimens during preliminary trials of heat treatment. According to Haynes et al., 21  investment casting techniques can be employed to produce shape-cast Al-Li alloys (with Li content up to 3.6 wt.%), which exhibit tensile properties comparable to those of commercial A356 alloy while achieving a density reduction down to 2.44 g/cm 3 . Seshan et al. 22  demonstrated that Al-Li, Al-Li-Mg, and Al-Li-Cu alloys can be effectively prepared by melting in an open atmosphere. To protect the molten metal from environmental interactions, a covering salt flux, a mixture of CaF 2  and CaCl 2 , was utilized. It was found that the hardness of the Al-3Li-1Mg alloy reached a peak of 138 HB after undergoing solution treatment at 550 °C for 1 hour, followed by quenching. Subsequent artificial aging at 170 °C reduced hardness to 120 HB after 5 hours, with recovery to the initial hardness level occurring only after 24 hours. At peak aging, the Al-3Li-1Cu alloy exhibited the highest Young’s modulus value of 9.4 × 10 4  MPa, with a density of 2.5 g/cm 3 , while the Al-3Li-1Mg alloy presented a slightly lower density of 2.48 g/cm 3  and Young’s modulus of 8.7 × 10 4  MPa.

Some authors use the most effective compositions of wrought alloys to develop materials suitable for shape casting. Numerous examples in the literature illustrate the effect of Li addition in the range of 0 to 2.9 wt.% on the structure and properties of Al-Cu alloys with varying copper content, 23 ,  24 – 25  as well as different alloying additions such as Sc, 26  Mg, 28  or Zr. 27  Guo et al. 29  discovered that an alloy composed of 2.5 wt.% Li, 2.0 wt.% Cu, 1.0 wt.% Mg, and 0.15 wt.% Zr, when cast into permanent steel molds, exhibited an impressive combination of strength and ductility. The yield strength reached 371 MPa, the ultimate tensile strength was 456 MPa, and the elongation was noted at 2.5 % in the peak-aged condition. In addition to these remarkable mechanical properties, all studied alloys displayed a tendency toward hot cracking, which is primarily associated with the broad solidification interval of Al-Cu alloys and the formation of undesirable Li-rich non-metallic inclusions such as Li 2 O, LiAlO 2 , LiH, and Li 2 CO 3 . This particular solidification behavior poses challenges for the production of thin-wall castings, particularly because these alloys are incompatible with high-pressure die casting (HPDC).

Another approach is to use a well-established casting alloy with the addition of Li. A review of the literature indicates that one of the most prominent casting alloys targeted for Li addition is AlSi7Mg (A356). In several studies conducted by Petric et al., Li was added to the AlSi7Mg casting alloy. 30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33  They identified the formation of a new Li-containing phase, AlLiSi, and attributed the alloy’s increased hardness to the precipitation of this phase’s primary particles within the α-Al matrix, alongside solid solution strengthening. 32  Furthermore, the authors examined the interactions between the AlSi7Mg+0.8 wt.%Li alloy melt and various mold materials. 30  They concluded that high casting quality is achieved when using steel or graphite molds. This conclusion is likely linked to the generation of differing gases (resulting from the thermal degradation of binders) when molten metal fills molds made from resin-coated sand or calcium silicate. Additionally, Chen et al. 34  identified a decrease in the Al-Si eutectic temperature of the A356 casting alloy upon the addition of 0.3 wt.% Li. This decrease is typically associated with eutectic modification, a finding corroborated by metallographic observations revealing the fibrous morphology of eutectic silicon in alloy cast into a permanent mold.

Previous publications by the authors have shown that the casting of Li-containing alloys can be designed based on the Al-Mg-Si system. 17  It was detected that the addition of 2.1 wt.% Li to an Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy can reduce the material density to 2,44 g/cm 3 , with a simultaneous increase in alloy hardness to 115 HV0.2, compared with 75 HV for the base alloy. It was also established that in the presence of Li an Al+Mg 2 Si eutectic formed in fine fibrous form instead of plate morphology of lamellas. In this paper, the authors present recent results on the structural characterization of an even higher Li-containing Al casting alloy, along with changes in mechanical properties in the as-cast condition.

sections.heading: Experimental Procedure
paragraphs: The chemical composition of the alloys examined corresponds to the Al5Mg2SiMn-type, as detailed in Table  1 . For the melting process, aluminum (Al 99.7% purity), magnesium (Mg 99.85%), and lithium (Li 99.9%) were utilized. Silicon and manganese were subsequently introduced by adding AlSi40 and AlMn20 master alloys. The melting operations were conducted in a resistance furnace equipped with a clay-graphite crucible. Throughout all experiments, the batch weight was 600 g, and the melt temperature was maintained at approximately 710 °C to reduce oxidation of Mg and Li. Before Li addition, the melt surface was covered with a LiF+LiCl flux pre-dried for 24 hours at 200°C. The molten alloy, at a temperature of 700°C, was cast into a permanent mold with a tetragonal cavity shape, as illustrated in Fig.  1 a. Liquid metal was poured directly into the mold from the top, preventing further oxidation within a gating system. The dimensions of the ingot were as follows: height—150 mm, width—40 mm, thickness—30 mm, resulting in an ingot weight of 300 g. The cooling behavior of the castings was estimated analytically using Chvorinov’s rule. 35  The casting geometry was 150 × 40 × 30 mm, and the mold material was medium-carbon steel with 10 mm wall thickness. The mold was assumed to be initially at 10 °C and exposed to ambient air with no coating on the inner surface. The initial parameters were as follows: casting volume V=1.8 × 10 −4  m 3 , cooling surface area A=0.0234 m 2 , mold constant B=0.7 s/mm 2 . Casting modulus was calculated from the casting volume and heat-extraction surface area M=V/A= 7.69 mm. The solidification interval was determined from differential scanning calorimetry measurements and was 585–630 °C. The estimated total solidification time was approximately 41 s, corresponding to an average cooling rate of approximately ~6 °C/s.

Following complete cooling, all ingots were sectioned in half for macrostructural observations. In Figure  1 a, the ingot after casting is depicted, and the ingot surface is clearly visible, which has the light gray color. Appearance of the light gray color specifies the partial oxidation of metal surface. The top part of the ingot containing shrinkage was cut down from the ingot before further processing. In Figure  1 b–d, the macrostructures of the Li0, Li0.8, and Li4.0 alloys are represented. All specimens, both with and without Li, exhibit an equiaxed structure extending from the bottom to the top. A small region at the bottom of the ingots features columnar crystals, as can be seen in Figure  1 d. The central portion of the ingots exhibits porosity. Despite using protective flux, this proved insufficient to prevent the metal from reacting with the surrounding oxidizing environment and airborne moisture. Porosity appeared in all cast samples independent on Li content. Thus, we performed microstructural analysis and mechanical testing only in areas with low porosity. In future, porosity shall be further reduced by improving the casting conditions. Alongside the macrostructural observations, further evidence of the absence of macro-segregation was obtained through hardness measurements taken from the longitudinal section of the ingots, as shown in Figure  1 e. The porous area was excluded from these measurements. The HV5 hardness of the Li0.8 alloy ranges from 95 to 105, which largely falls within the measurement error. From this analysis, one can conclude that, at the macroscopic level, the cast ingots exhibit no segregation of alloying elements and maintain a relatively uniform structure.

The specimens subjected to metallographic analysis were sectioned from the central regions of the ingots, deliberately avoiding areas with concentrated porosity. For microstructure characterization, these samples were mounted in electrically conductive hot-mounting resin and subjected to standard metallographic procedures, including grinding and polishing with a diamond suspension in conjunction with a non-oxidizing alcohol-based lubricant, followed by vibration polishing with a silica-based oxide polishing suspension (OPS). The use of electrically conductive hot-mounting resin is necessary for further examination of specimens using a scanning electron microscope.

Special attention was given to ensuring the complete removal of OPS remnants from the specimen’s surface. Immediately after polishing, the specimens were immersed in a solution of Micro Organic Soap and cleaned in an ultrasonic bath. Following cleaning, the specimens were examined under light microscopy and subsequently etched in a 6% NaOH solution at 40 °C for 30 seconds. To reveal the morphology of individual phases, deep etching techniques were employed. A 10% NaOH solution in distilled water was used for the deep etching process, which was conducted at 20 °C for 30 minutes, after which the samples were briefly cleaned in a 0.1% HCl solution. The grain size was measured on specimens that had been mechanically ground, polished, and anodized using Barker’s reagent (20 V, 100 s) with a LectroPol-5 Electrolytic Polishing Machine.

Following preparation, the microstructure of the samples in the as-cast condition was examined using a Leica DMA 5000M light microscope in conjunction with IMagic IMS image capture and analysis software. Anodized specimens were examined under polarized light with a sensitive color filter. To investigate phases, morphology, and composition, a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, MERLIN® VP Compact, Co. Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray (EDS) detector (XFlash 6/30, Co. Bruker, Berlin, Germany) was employed. The resin-embedded samples were coated with a 5.0-nm-thick layer of carbon (CCU-010, Co. Safematic GmbH, Zizers, Switzerland) and mounted directly onto the sample carrier using conductive carbon tape.

A representative area from each sample was analyzed and mapped for elemental distribution based on the EDS spectra data, utilizing Quantax Esprit Microanalysis software (version 2.0). During EDS measurements, a series of tests was conducted to determine a suitable accelerating voltage for detecting the specific alloy composition and especially to reveal Mg concentration in α-Al solid solution grains.

The accelerating voltage ranged from 3 to 20 kV, and the results are illustrated in Figure  2 . Analysis points are numbered 1 to 6, with the measured Mg content plotted against the accelerating voltage in Figure  2 b. In accordance with established EDS practice, the beam energy should be at least twice the Kα line energy, which for Mg is 1.25 keV; thus, a suitable accelerating voltage should be approximately 2 to 2.5 kV. However, at 3 kV, the quantification resulted in only 1.35 wt.% Mg (spectrum collected for 60 seconds from point 1), which is an underestimation due to insufficient beam energy to excite the Mg Kα line. Elevating the voltage to the moderate range of 5 to 10 kV yielded reliable results, with Mg content in the matrix ranging from 2.7 to 2.9 wt.% (points 2, 3, 4), representing the most accurate data obtained. Moreover, further increasing the voltage led to a gradual escalation in Mg concentration, peaking at 4.0 wt.% at 20 kV, attributable to the expansion of the interaction volume. The potential presence of Mg 2 Si beneath the specimen’s surface must also be considered. Based on these measurements, all EDS analyses were performed at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. Figure 2 Results of quantification of EDS analysis of Mg content in α-Al matrix vs accelerating voltage used.

For X-ray structural studies, a Rigaku Ultima IV diffractometer (Cu Kα radiation, λ =0.15406 nm) was used, with an angular range of 2θ = 10 − 120°, a registration step of 0.04°, and an exposure time of 2 seconds at each point. The quantitative phase composition of the alloys was calculated from the integrated intensities of non-overlapping diffraction maxima typical for each phase, using the Rietveld approach realized in the PDXL software. The phase composition was refined by fitting structural models from the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), along with refining scale factors, lattice parameters, diffraction maximum profiles, and background. The pseudo-Voigt profile function and polynomial background modeling were applied. Based on X-ray diffraction results, the quantitative phase composition, the size of the coherent scattering domains (CSD), and the degree of crystal lattice deformation (ε) were determined.

Hardness tests were performed using the KB 30SR hardness testing machine (KB Prüftechnik GmbH, Germany) with a load of 5.0 kg. Five parallel measurements were applied for each sample. Compression yield strength R p0.2  was measured in a quenching/deformation dilatometer DIL 805A/D (TA Instruments, New Castle, DE, USA) on cylindrical specimens with a length of 10 mm and a diameter of 5 mm at room and 300 °C temperatures. The cast material volume has not been sufficient for tensile testing. Thus, we focused on hardness and compression tests. We are aware of this restriction, and results from compression test should only carefully be compared with tensile properties.

sections.heading: Characterization of Phases in Base AlMg5Si2Mn-Type Alloys
paragraphs: Three specimens were selected as the base alloys for this study (Table  1 ). The first specimen, designated as Li0 (2011), is an Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy that was cast in a permanent mold. It is important to note that this alloy was cast in 2011. The specimens have undergone natural aging for 14 years. The second alloy, labeled as Li0, was also cast in the same permanent mold (PM) but contained a higher Fe content of 0.31 wt.% compared with 0.05 wt.% in the Li0 (2011). This alloy was cast in December 2024, and the specimens were stored in a refrigerator at – 25 °C to slow down natural aging. The third specimen, Li0 HPDC, was a 3-mm-thick plate that was high-pressure die cast.

Figure  3 a-c illustrates the overall grain morphology obtained through Barker etching of the specimens of base alloys. A comparison of the structures reveals significant differences in the α-Al grain morphology among the three alloys. For the Li0 and Li0 (2011) alloys, a dendritic structure with well-developed primary and secondary arms of α-Al is observed, whereas the morphology of α-Al in the HPDC alloy is mainly spherical. Figure 3 Grain morphology observed in experimental alloys under polarized light after Barker etching.

Figure  4  summarizes the microstructural investigation conducted on both the PM and HPDC cast alloys. It can be concluded that the grains of the α-Al solid solution, as well as the eutectic structure of the Li0 HPDC alloy, are significantly finer than those observed in castings produced using a permanent mold. The average α-Al grain size of the die-cast specimen was measured at 15 ± 3 μm, characterized by a spherical morphology and surrounded by fine fibrous lamella of Mg 2 Si intermetallic. The average interlamellar spacing can be estimated to range from 110 nm to 170 nm. In contrast, the average grain size of the Li0 (2011) specimen is 230 ± 10 μm, with the lamellar morphology plate-like, as illustrated in Figure  4 b and d. Figure 4 Microstructure of base alloys Al5Mg2SiMn-type without Li.

It is well established that Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloys are based on the Al-Mg-Si system with a pseudo-binary section and comprise two major constituents: α-Al solid solution grains and the α-Al+Mg 2 Si eutectic. In HPDC, solidification begins with the nucleation of α-Al grains, followed by the formation of eutectic colonies. This sequence of phase formation is evident in Figure  4 e, where fibrous eutectic colonies surround spherical α-Al grains. However, in PM alloys that cool more slowly than HPDC, even with similar compositions, the phase formation sequence somewhat changes. It begins with the development of primary faceted Mg 2 Si crystals at the centers of the eutectic colonies, as illustrated in Figure  4 a and c. Concurrently, α-Al nucleates and grows within a nearly identical temperature range. The final phase to solidify is the α-Al+Mg 2 Si eutectic, consisting of Mg 2 Si intermetallic plates alternating with α-Al. In the case of alloy Li0, the solidification sequence is slightly modified by the presence of 0.31 wt.% Fe, leading to the formation of blocky-shaped crystals containing Fe + Mn at the early stage of crystallization as shown in Figure  5 b. Figure 5 X-ray diffraction pattern of Li0 alloy, and morphology of α-Al 15 (Fe,Mn) 3 Si 2  phase.

The average chemical composition of the phases in the Li0 (2011) specimen was determined by EDS analysis at an accelerating voltage of 5.0 kV. The resulting mean values of the α-Al matrix were 1.79 wt.% Mg, 1.03 wt.% Si, and 0.26 wt.% Mn. The maximum Mg content recorded was 2.57 wt.%, while the minimum was 0.97 wt.%. Using an accelerating voltage of 5 kV does not provide reliable information on the concentrations of Si, Mn, and Fe, as excitation at this voltage primarily occurs in the L-series of these elements. However, as demonstrated in the previous section (Figure  2 b), Mg content can be quantified with high accuracy. The matrix composition of the Li0 alloy does not significantly differ from that of Li0 (2011). The average Mg content was 2.30 wt.%, with a range of 2.64–1.87 wt.%. In the case of the Li0 HPDC alloy, the matrix’s chemical composition slightly varies from that of the PM alloys. The average Mg content was 2.72 wt.%. Si concentrations ranged from 1.45 to 0.50 wt.%. Mn varied between 0.45 and 0.62 wt.%. The HPDC’s higher cooling rate for 3 mm thickness could be estimated to be in the range of 100–120 K s -1 , resulting in higher Mg and Si contents than in PM specimens. The measured Mn content in the solid solution closely matches the total Mn content added to the melt, indicating that only a small fraction of the Mn enters iron-containing phases.

Using data obtained from EDS measurements, the so-called effective partition coefficient of Mg during solidification of Al-Mg-Si alloy can be estimated using the formula  k eff  = C max /C 0 , using the approach proposed by Easton et al. 36  In this equation,  k eff  represents the “effective” partition coefficient, C max  denotes the maximum measured concentration of Mg, i.e., 2.57 wt.% for the Li0 (2011) alloy, and C 0  refers to the average Mg content in the alloy (5.46 wt.%, see Table  1 ). Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements indicate that the solidification onset temperature for the Li0 (2011) alloy is 620 °C, aligning well with findings reported by Warmuzek et al. 37  At this temperature, grains of the α-Al solid solution and Mg 2 Si primary phase undergo nucleation and growth, reaching a peak temperature of 618 °C. The latter consumes part of Mg from the α-Al. The solid solution predominates in the dendritic structure at slow cooling rates (permanent mold casting), whereas under high cooling rates, it maintains a spherical structure, typical of high-pressure die casting (HPDC). The partition coefficient,  k eff , has been estimated at 0.47 for PM casting. For the HPDC alloy,  k eff  is slightly higher, at 0.5. The equilibrium value of  k e  for Al-Mg alloys is 0.45, indicating that at relatively slow cooling rates of Al-Mg-Si alloys,  k eff  of Mg is nearly equal to  k e . Conversely, with moderate cooling rates,  k eff  increases due to incomplete partitioning and solute trapping at the interface. Results of EDS measurements of the composition of solid solution for base alloys are summarized in Table  2 , together with calculated  k eff . Table 2 Composition of α-Al Solid Solution Grains Measured by EDS in Base Alloys Alloy Overall Mg content in the alloy, wt.% Max measured Mg content in α-Al, wt.% Average Mg content in α-Al, wt.% k eff Li0 (2011) 5.46 2.57 1.79 0.47 Li0 5.65 2.64 2.30 0.46 Li0 HPDC 5.45 2.97 2.72 0.50

The results from X-ray diffraction studies of the three base alloys revealed the presence of at least two distinct phases, clearly identifiable from the spectra presented in Figure  5 a. These phases include fcc α-Al, characterized by a lattice parameter (LP) of  a  = 0.4059 nm, and fcc Mg 2 Si, with a lattice parameter of  a  = 0.6339 nm (see Table  4 ). Additionally, in the Li0 alloy containing 0.31 wt.% Fe, a Fe-bearing phase was identified. This is the primary bcc α-Al 15 (Fe,Mn) 3 Si 2  phase, exhibiting a LP of  a  = 1.2686 nm and a compact polyhedral morphology, as illustrated in Figure  4 b. The EDS analysis revealed the composition of this phase as follows: Al 67.01 wt.%, Si 9.92 wt.%, Mn 15.40 wt.%, Fe 7.67 wt.%. A summary of the LP and weight fractions of phases is provided in Table  3  in the following section.

sections.heading: Characterization of Phases in Base AlMg5Si2Mn-Type Alloys Containing Li
paragraphs: Li content in experimental alloys ranged from 0.88 to 4.0 wt.% as mentioned in Table  1 . Results of microstructural studies of the first Li-containing specimen, Li 0.8, are summarized in Figure  6 a-i. Similar to the base alloys, the specimen’s structure consists of α-Al, as shown in Figure  6 a, surrounded by eutectic colonies. Part of the eutectic exhibits fine fibrous structure, as shown in Figure  6 b, while others are plate-like, depicted in Figure  6 c. In the center of the plate-like eutectic, the primary crystal exhibited octahedron morphology. The EDS mapping reveals that the two types of eutectics—plate-like (marked 1 in Figure  6 c) and fine dispersed needles (marked 2 in Figure  6 c)—exhibit distinct compositions. The intermetallics in the plate-like eutectic are predominantly composed of Si and Mg (as shown in Figure  6 e and f) and can be identified as Mg 2 Si. The presence of Mg 2 Si was also confirmed by X-ray diffraction studies (see Table  4 ). Figure 6 Structure of Li0.8 alloy and EDS mapping of Mg, Si, Fe, Mn, and EDS spectrum obtained from primary crystal in the center of plate-like eutectic colony.

Meanwhile, the intermetallics in the fine fibrous eutectic are enriched by Fe, Mn and Si (Figure  6 f, g, h) and belong to Al(Fe,Mn)Si quaternary Al-rich system. EDS measurements of separate particles of this compound gave Al 63.2 wt.%, Si 9.1 wt.%, Mn 19.0 wt.%, and Fe 8.7 wt.%, which fits to the α-Al 15 (Fe,Mn) 3 Si 2  intermetallic. Its fine morphology, probably, originated from the modifying effect of Li. The core of a plate-like eutectic colony comprises a primary crystal, as shown in Figure  6 d and f. Quantitative EDS analysis indicated that the crystal is primarily composed of 32.2 wt.% Al and 66.8 wt.% Si (Figure  6 i). Additionally, trace amounts of Mn, Fe, and Mg were detected, although their concentrations are below 0.5 wt.% and are likely influenced by the surrounding matrix. According to the established binary Al-Si phase diagram, 38  such a phase does not exist. Therefore, the most relevant hypothesis is that the crystal is the primary AlLiSi phase. Due to the low atomic mass of Li, its detection by EDS is not feasible. This phase was also determined by X-ray diffraction and is reported in Table  3 . Its fraction is relatively low, at 1 wt.%. The appearance of the primary AlLiSi crystal in the center of the eutectic colony specifies that the growth of the eutectic plates starts from it. Also, Zeka et al. in course of phases identification in Al7SiMg+Li alloy proposed that a phase containing approximately 50 wt.% Si and a corresponding amount of Al do not exist in an Al-Si alloy. Consequently, they concluded that a new phase appears in the AlSi7Mg alloy upon the addition of 0.8 wt.% Li is the AlLiSi phase. 31

Increasing the Li content to 2.1 wt.% (alloy Li2.1) results in the complete elimination of the fine-lamellar eutectic structure. As illustrated in Figure  7 , there are no lamellas formed. Instead, coarser blocky intermetallic particles are formed. When examining the morphology of these particles, most observed crystals are octahedral (see Figure  7 b) and are randomly distributed within the matrix. The distance between individual crystals ranges from 9 to 15 µm. Additionally, some agglomeration of particles is noted, as shown in Figure  7 a and b, where the distance between certain crystals is approximately 1–2 µm. Based on the EDS analysis, it is evident that the composition of the crystals varies from one another. The elements distribution indicates that Mg (Figure  7 f) is primarily concentrated in the α-Al matrix, with an average content of 3.5 wt.%. Fe is found predominantly in the irregularly shaped particles, with their composition quantified as Al 63.6 wt.%, Si 7.7 wt.%, Mn 10.4 wt.%, and Fe 18.0 wt.%. A third phase was observed with an increase in Mn and Si intensities. The chemical composition of this phase was determined to be 39.9 wt.% Si, 59.3 wt.% Mn, and 0.7 wt.% Al. If we consider that a minor amount of Al may be present as an effect from the surrounding matrix, the resulting Mn/Si ratio becomes 60:40. This composition aligns more closely to Mn-silicide and lie between MnSi and Mn 4 Si 7 , but closer to MnSi. Based on the EDS measurements, this particle may be identified as Si-rich MnSi-type phase. Within the structure of the Li2.1 alloy, the crystals of this phase display a blocky morphology with sharp edges, as depicted at the center of Figure  7 b. The presence of the MnSi phase in the alloy was confirmed via X-ray diffraction examinations (see Table  3 ). Figure 7 Structure of Li2.1 alloy and EDS mapping of Si, Fe, Mg, and Mn specifying the presence of Mn–Si–rich particles.

Further increasing the Li content to 2.5 wt.% produced a similar effect: The eutectic structure fully changed toward coarser blocky intermetallics embedded in an Al matrix, with no evidence of eutectic colonies. As shown in Figure  8 , microstructural analysis of the Li2.5 alloy indicated that its main constituent is blocky crystals, averaging 2-5 µm, embedded in the α-Al matrix. EDS analysis of various crystals revealed that one blocky-type crystal, similarly to Li2.1 alloy, exhibits a composition of 74.2 wt.% Mn and 21.5 wt.% Si, with minor intensities of Al and Mg also detected. This composition corresponds to the MnSi phase, which possesses a stoichiometric composition of 83 wt.% Mn and 17 wt.% Si. Figure 8 Structure of Li2.5 alloy.

Further increasing the Li content to 3.0 wt.% resulted in a structure similar to that of the Li2.5 alloy. The results of microstructural studies are summarized in Figure  8 , which shows the complete disappearance of eutectic structures. As shown in Figure  9 a and b, the structure contains mainly large, faceted crystals. EDS spectra of these crystals revealed Mg and Si, and the element content was measured as Mg 43.3 wt.% and Si 55.2 wt.%. Despite the Mg/Si ratio being close to 1/1, these crystals may be identified as Mg 2 Si primary intermetallic. It is worth noting that all primary Mg 2 Si particles contain internal cracks, indicating their brittleness. Together with cracks, marked by an arrow in Figure  8 c, branched white lines cover nearly the entire surface of the crystal. The most obvious supposition is that these lines are a cleavage network. Cracks were revealed inside Mg 2 Si after conventional grinding and polishing, as well as in crystals observed after deep etching, where no stress was applied to the surface. This indicates that the cracks formed during solidification and cooling of the alloy in the mold cavity due to the difference in the thermal expansion of α-Al 22×10 -6  K -1  and Mg 2 Si 7.5×10 -6  K -1 . Figure 9 Structure of Li3.0 alloy and EDS mapping of Mg, Si, Mn, and Fe.

The Li4.0 alloy exhibited the highest lithium content among the specimens studied. Its structure again consists of coarse faceted polyhedral crystals, which indicate primary crystallization from the melt. These crystals display well-developed flat faces and sharp edges. All crystals are randomly distributed in the α-Al matrix. Similar to the Li3.0 alloy, some crystals have cracks in Li4.0 alloy, as shown in Figure  10 b. Despite the close morphology of all displayed crystals, EDS analysis revealed differences between them. Figure  10  represents the EDS mapping of Si (d), Mg (e), and Mn (f) together with the combined image of Si+Mg (g). Comparing the areas with high Si and Mg intensity, one can see that Si is present in nearly all crystals across the analyzed area, whereas Mg is only detected in some crystals. EDS point analysis showed that some Mg-rich areas contained 61.3 wt.% Mg and 33.2 wt.% Si, which closely matches Mg 2 Si (Figure  10 h). The positions of these crystals are marked by arrows. Other particles with Si concentration showed a Si content of 84.2 wt.%, Al-14.5 wt.%, and Mg-1.3 wt.%, which is most likely is AlLiSi phase (Figure  10 h). AlLiSi has also been confirmed by XRD (Table  3 ). The third type of crystals contains 75.3 wt.% Mn and 22.6 wt.% Si, specified as the MnSi phase (Figure  10 i). Figure 10 Structure of Li4.0 alloy and EDS mapping of Si, Mg, Mn, and combined EDS mapping of Si+Mg, morphology of AlLiSi and Mg 2 Si phases, and Mn 5 Si 2 .

Table  3  summarizes the microstructure evolution with increasing Li content. The solidification of Al–Mg 2 Si alloys without lithium is primarily governed by the eutectic reaction L → α-Al + Mg 2 Si. According to the quasi-binary phase diagram Al–Mg 2 Si, this eutectic solidification takes place around 580-590 °C. Adding 1.7 to 1.9 wt.% lithium to the alloy system changes the solidification path toward L → α-Al + AlLiSi. In this case, Mg 2 Si forms afterward at lower temperatures. 39 , 40  Similar modifications have been reported for the solidification path of Al7SiMg in the presence of 0.8 wt.% lithium. It changes from L → α-Al + Si at 577 °C toward L → α-Al + AlLiSi, and the Si phase forms later at lower temperatures. 33  At lower lithium content of 0.1 to 0.3 wt.% in Al7SiMg, the solidification path remains L → α-Al + Si, but the eutectic temperature decreases and the α-Al + Si morphology changes from plate-like to spherical. 34  These lithium-caused modifications of the solidification path and especially the lower formation temperature of Mg 2 Si in Al-Mg-Si-Li alloys are assumed to contribute to the changes from plate-like to blocky-type Mg 2 Si. sections.heading: X-ray Diffraction Studies of Li-Containing Alloys
paragraphs: Table  4  and Figure  11  present the X-ray diffraction results, detailing existing phases, lattice constants, and phase fractions of the experimental alloys. In the Li0 alloy, lattice parameter (LP) of the fcc α-Al solid solution was measured as  a =0.4059 nm, which is slightly higher than that obtained for pure Al (99.99 purity,  a =0.4042 nm). For Mg-containing alloys, according to Li et al., 41  an increase in Mg content up to 2.0 wt.% leads to a change of the Al lattice constant to 0.40530 nm, which is close to that detected for Li0 alloy, where the concentration of Mg in the solid solution is 2.6 wt.%. Increasing Li content to 0.8 wt.% reduced the LP to 0.40544 nm, suggesting Li replaced Mg in the α-Al lattice, leading to a decrement of the LP. Further Li addition expanded the lattice to 0.40621 nm at 3.0 wt. % Li and, simultaneously, decreased the α-Al fraction from 79 wt.% in the Li0 alloy to 66 wt.% in the Li3.0 specimen. Lowering the fraction of α-Al is attributed to the formation and enlargement of the fraction of AlLiSi and AlLi phases. For the second major phase, Mg 2 Si, the LP of the base alloy Li0 was measured to be  a =0.63510 nm and its weight fraction was determined as 8 wt.%. This value is close to the stoichiometric calculation, which yields approximately 6 wt.% Mg 2 Si. Increasing the Li content caused the lattice to expand to 0.639 nm in the Li3.0 alloy, then decrease to 0.63684 nm. Concurrently, the Mg 2 Si fraction initially increased from 8.0 wt.% to 14 wt.% in the Li2.5 alloy and then decreased to 6.0 wt.%.

Li-containing phases were identified in all alloys except Li0 and Li0.8. AlLiSi phase was assumed as the primary crystal at the center of the eutectic colony in the Li0.8 alloy (Figure  6 d), but was not identified via X-ray studies in this alloy. It is likely due to its low fraction in the alloy. Further Li addition led to a gradual increase in the AlLiSi phase fraction, reaching a maximum of 6 wt.%, and its crystals were found in the structure of the Li4.0 specimen, as shown in Figure  10 h. This observation supports the existence of the phase and its incremental increase in all Li-containing specimens. A similar trend was observed for the primary AlLi phase, with a weight fraction less than 5 wt% in the Li2.1 alloy and increasing to 9 wt.% in the Li4.0 alloy. It is also worth noting that the LP for the AlLi phase was measured of 0.417 nm in the Li2.1 specimen, following continuous growth up to 0.494 nm in the Li4.0 alloy. In contrast, the behavior of the fraction of α - Al 15 (Fe,Mn) 3 Si 2  phase showed a slow decline from 12 wt.% down to 8 wt.% in the Li4.0 specimen.

A notable observation was the presence of a MnSi phase in the X-ray diffraction patterns of all alloys examined in this study, except Li0. Faceted polyhedral crystals composed exclusively of MnSi were identified in the Li4.0 specimen, as shown in Figure  10 i, along with their composition determined by EDS. Although information on the formation of the MnSi phase in Al-rich environments remains limited, its identification by EDS and XRD substantiates its presence. Further investigation is required to clarify the compositional and temperature conditions that facilitate the formation of the MnSi phase. According to the investigations of Krendelsberger et al. 42  in the Al-Mn-Si ternary system, MnSi is an equilibrium compound and may be formed. The condition of formation of this phase in Al-Mg-Si-Mn, where Mn content is on the level of 0.6 wt.%, is not clearly understood, and probably the formation of MnSi crystals results from non-equilibrium conditions during solidification. According to Long et al., 43  the Li-Mn-Si phase diagram does not indicate the existence of any ternary compounds.

Summarizing, phases α-Al, Mg 2 Si, and α-Al 15 (Fe,Mn) 3 Si 2  could clearly be identified by EDS and XRD. Further, we have found strong indications for the existence of phases MnSi, AlLiSi, and δ-AlLi, which should be confirmed in future work.

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties of Li-Containing Alloys
paragraphs: Hardness tests were conducted on all specimens in the as-cast condition to evaluate their mechanical properties. The results of HV5 hardness measurements for the alloys in the as-cast state are presented in Figure  12 a. HV5 load was selected to ensure that the measured hardness reflects contributions from all constituent phases. Figure  12 b represents the view of indentation in Li0 alloy where the indenter touches not only α-Al, but the eutectic colonies. The base alloy Li0 exhibited an average hardness of 83 HV, and the addition of 0.8 wt.% Li did not result in a significant change. However, further increases in Li content to 3.0 and 4.0 wt.% produce a remarkable rise in hardness, reaching 158 HV5 on average for the Li4.0 alloy. Figure 12 Mechanical properties of experimental alloys.

Microhardness tests were employed to characterize the mechanical properties of individual phases. As can be seen from Figure  12 c, the measurements of Vickers hardness done at the load of HV0.05 gave results, which slightly differ from that of HV5. For base alloy Li0, the α-Al matrix was found of 71 HV0.05, whereas HV5 was found of 83. This difference of 12 HV specifies the contribution of intermetallics to the hardness of the material. Effect of Li addition on the HV0.05 showed a similar tendency as it was observed in HV5 measurements. Difference in HV0.05 for Li0 and Li4.0 alloys is equal to 71 HV on average and shows the strengthening effect of Li on the alloy matrix.

Results of compression tests are summarized in Figure  12 e. Tests were performed at room temperature and at 300 °C. The Li additions in the range of 0.8 to 2.5 wt.% do not significantly affect the yield strength (YS), which remains between 135 MPa for the Li0 alloy and 148 MPa for Li2.5. A substantial increase in YS is observed for alloys containing 3.0 and 4.0 wt.% Li. Consistent with the hardness measurements, the YS of these alloys at room temperature nearly doubles, reaching about 352 MPa, compared with that of the Li-free material. At 300 °C, the YS increases gradually from 124 MPa for the Li0 alloy to 170 MPa for Li4.0. Alloys L2.1, Li2.5, Li3, and Li4 contain a higher Mg content than the other alloys. Thus, higher Mg content may also contribute to higher strength. However, the increase in hardness and yield strength of Li3.0 and Li4.0 alloys compared to L2.1 and Li2.5 cannot be directly attributed to differences in Mg content. Double improvement of YS and hardness is not the action of Mg alone. It can mostly be related to the presence of Li.

Numerous researchers have thoroughly examined the mechanical properties of the Al5Mg2SiMn-type casting alloy suitable for HPDC. One of the first data sources was the publication by Koch et al. 44  The YS of the alloy with nominal composition Al5Mg2SiMn subjected to HPDC was found to be 190 ± 10 MPa, accompanied by relative elongation (RE) of 17 % at a wall thickness of 2–3 mm and temper F. According to technical information published in 2017, 45  the YS of an HPDC AlMg5Si2Mn-type alloy for wall thicknesses less than 2 mm is reported to be 220 MPa. The same YS value is observed in a modified version of this alloy containing Zr and Mo. In the works of Hu et al. and others, 46 ,  47 ,  48 – 49  it was observed that the YS of HPDC Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy depends on the Mg content. Increasing Mg content from 5.7 to 7.2 wt.%, keeping Si at a level of 1.9 wt.%, leads to improvement of YS from 183 MPa to 200 MPa in the as-cast condition. 46  Later, by comparing the mechanical properties of this alloy cast by HPDC and PM, 47  it was found that the YS of the HPDC alloy (189 MPa) differed significantly from that of the PM alloy (111 MPa). The YS of the PM alloy is not substantially different from that of the Li0 alloy, at 135 MPa. Ji et al. 47  attributed the low mechanical properties of the PM alloy to a coarse-grain size, the presence of shrinkage pores, and the effect of Fe-rich brittle intermetallics. The coarse-grain size, which is also observed in the present studies (see Figure  3 b and j), resulted from the relatively low cooling rate of permanent mold casting in comparison with HPDC (see Figure  3 g). Recent data published by Chen et al. 50  explored the variations of Mg/Si ratio on the properties of Al-Mg-Si-Mn cast alloy where it was proven that the YS gradually increases with lowering Mg/Si. For alloy with Mg/Si = 2.83, which is close to Li0 alloy in the present study, the measured YS was detected at 159 MPa, keeping in mind that the alloy was cast into copper mold and the cooling rate was found of 137.5 K s -1 , which is even higher than that for thin sections in HPDC. In addition, the direct aging of HPDC Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy at a temperature of 250°C may increase YS to 238 MPa. 47

The body of publications that dealt with the Li effect on the properties of cast Al-Mg-Si alloys is somewhat limited. One of the first attempts to design materials for the Al-Mg-Si-Li system is the work of W. Romero. 51  It was found that the YS of a rolled sheet of the Al4.3Mg1.1Si3.1Li alloy in the artificially aged conditions was the highest, at 270 MPa. Hadian et al. 52 , 53  detected the addition of 0.3 wt.% Li to Al-Mg 2 Si composite leads to an increase in ultimate tensile strength (UTS) in the as-cast condition from 160 to 200 MPa with a simultaneous rise in elongation.

The summarized data on the mechanical properties, particularly YS, of Al5Mg2SiMn-type casting alloy with Li clearly indicate that the present Li3.0 and Li4.0 alloys exhibit considerable superiority in the as-cast condition compared with the state of the art. Table  5  compares the mechanical properties of Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy with Li against commercial Al5Mg2SiMn alloys as well as Al7SiMg alloys. This specifies the effectiveness of Li addition in improving the mechanical properties of this alloy. An increase in YS at elevated temperatures is also noticeable and beneficial for the material. Comparisons between compression test results and tensile properties must be performed carefully, and tensile tests will be conducted in the future. Preliminary cost estimation indicated that the actual price for Al commercial purity is about 3.7 US dollars per kg. Adding the costs of Mg, Si, and Mn of 3.5 US dollars per kg, the resulting materials cost of the Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy can be estimated at about 4.0 US dollars per kg. The price of Li is currently about 45 dollars per kg. The maximum Li addition studied was 4.0 wt.% Li. Thus, the material cost increased to about 5.5 US dollars per kg -1 , which is equivalent to 37% increase. Manufacturing costs will increase further due to challenges in processing Al-Li-alloys. Although Li increases alloy costs, the resulting reduction in structural weight and increase in specific strength may offset these costs for weight-critical applications.

In this paper, the authors will not discuss the strengthening mechanisms that contribute to the overall increase in the mechanical properties of the alloys studied. Solid solution strengthening due to the presence of high solute content of Mg and Li, newly formed intermetallics AlLi, AliLiSi, and MnSi, as well as Li-containing nano-precipitates will contribute to the overall strength improvement. Further, changing its structure from eutectic-type to coarser blocky intermetallics within the α-Al matrix will play a role. Strengthening mechanisms and solidification paths will be the focus of further research.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The results presented above indicate that the Al-Mg-Si-Mn system is a promising candidate for the design of Li-containing casting alloys with high strength and reduced density, achievable in the as-cast condition without artificial aging. Melting and casting of the alloy can be performed in an open atmosphere, thereby eliminating the need for vacuum or inert-gas furnaces. The key findings are summarized as follows: The addition of lithium up to 4 wt.% induces significant microstructural changes in the Al5Mg2SiMn-type alloy. Above 2.1 wt.% Li, the formation of eutectic lamellas or fibers is entirely suppressed and only coarser blocky intermetallics are formed. Alongside α-Al and primary Mg 2 Si phases, we have found strong indications for two lithium-containing intermetallics, AlLiSi and AlLi at higher Li content. These intermetallics exhibit coarse, faceted polyhedral crystal morphologies, indicating primary crystallization from the melt. Further, MnSi-intermetallics have been observed. When the Li content amounts 4 wt.%, the Al-Mg-Si-Mn-type alloy exhibits high hardness, reaching up to 157 HV5, as well as high compressive yield strength up to 352 MPa. Both hardness and yield strength at least double those of the lithium-free alloy. Even elevated-temperature compression tests at 300°C show a yield strength of about 170 MPa. Comparison between results from compression tests and tensile properties must be performed carefully, and tensile tests will be conducted in future. Based on these results, it can be concluded that Al5Mg2SiMn-type casting alloys with additions of up to 4 wt.% Li are very promising materials for future lightweight design. To fully understand and explore these excellent properties, further research will be conducted on the specific solidification paths leading to the described microstructures and on the strengthening mechanisms responsible for the high yield strength. Probably, solid solution strengthening as well as Li-containing nano-precipitates will play a role.
